title: Can you actually predict the stock market?
author: Weird_Cookie1700
selftext:
Yes. You can.

[This is my ROI off paper trades from last week. I use my trading sessions as teaching tools for Charles 2.0. Anybody can do this.](https://preview.redd.it/os8afa91g6sh1.png?width=1196&format=png&auto=webp&s=20984cc7a6b2a382047001ec28ed66a3ff834b1f)

The first version that could do it was called Charles, he predicted whether a stock was going to up or down from it's open price. He had a 98% prediction accuracy for that and I thought that was amazing until I dug into the numbers.

Charles was counting the price of a stock going above just a penny, or a fraction, over open as accurate, which, in his defense was actually what I asked him to do. But that was unacceptable.

I did find out that his accuracy for predicting whether a stock would hit certain percentages was not too shabby.

.25% gain - 89% of the time the stock he chose went .25% above open during the trading day  
.5% gain - 65% of the time the stock he chose went .5% above open during the trading day  
1% gain - .34% of the time the stock he chose went 1% above open during the trading day

I thought, I can work with that, and built Charles 2.0 as a prediction monster.

91.9% - prediction accuracy for a stock gaining .5% during the trading day  
84.6% - prediction accuracy for a stock gaining 1% during the trading day

Now, this is where we need to clarify some things.

Charles was live on Android and iOS from March until early September, had 3k+ users, and hundreds of those actually used Charles to buy and sell stocks as well as set trails, reversals, limits, etc. There was a lot that Charles did and there was a LOT of data we were able to capture because of it.

Charles had 3 different strategies that players could choose from and Charles had 17 that he was constanty updating based on the players and the data we were capturing for Charles.

It was a beautiful thing, but we had to shut it down, take it off the stores and web, in order to do a full rebuild basically.

Thats how Charles 2.0 was created.

We took all of the data we'd gained during those live months, dissected it every which way we could imagine, and built from that data.

[I had to black out a few things, you know, secret sauce kind of stuff.](https://preview.redd.it/2yjf9wp3e6sh1.png?width=1190&format=png&auto=webp&s=2167f2d3aabb1b5bc16e1f075c863c36beaa418f)

Charles 2.0 has only been alive for 1 week, but he's performing nicely so far and we should see improved results this week.

I literally just created a new algorithm that piggybacks off his current strategy to achieve much better results while I was typing this. We'll see what the real world says tomorrow at open though.

So, how does Charles do it?

I think at this point he uses about 17 different signals, some signals are weighted differently based on the market, and he uses a specific stock universe (I think this is a key part) tailored to the specific way I trade. So he's not using every stock out there, he's already cherry picked his best stocks (and I think there's about 300 in his universe) and he just uses those everyday.

There's also his enter strategy, exit strategy, times he buys, what he does when he's not buying, how he reacts throughout the day to what he's seeing going on, tons of things. But they're all things I came up with using logic.

1. I don't know how to code.  
2. I don't know half as much about stocks as I should.

All I know is what I learned from watching the market. Stock prices go up, stock prices go down. I used logic to figure out how to trade and then I used that logic to make it automated (Charles just wants to take some baby steps right now I guess).

I've made hundreds of algorithms probably, and most of them work, it just depends on how well they work you know? And if you make an algorithm based off of another, even a clone, sometimes they won't act the same, so you want to test as much as you can on everything you can possibly think of. You want to be your own worst critic.

And let's face it, most everybody is using AI to build whatever AI is going to trade so I'm hoping we all know at this point that we have to guide them, but we have to do it in a way that doesn't compromise our results, especially our live results.

These are my steps for creating an algorithm:

\- I have a theory, I test it using Cursor, I test it about a hundred different ways because I know it was just being lazy when it said my theory sucked the first time.

\- Along the way I usually modify what I'm looking for as far as entering and exiting based on what I'm seeing in the results. I just adjust accordingly but I'm always keeping in mind that I can't compromise the data and make it biased.

\- If it survives that I'm probably going to make a test account out of it and track it for a few weeks to see how it's doing. While that's going on, if I see something I need to change or tweak, I'll do so, but I'll do it on a copy of the original so I'm never messing with what I aleady have running. I think a lot of people adjust what may already be working, they just didn't give it enough time.

\- Once the testing period is done, and that's determined on a case by case basis, the strategy gets moved to live testing on an Alpaca paper account for a few weeks to determine slippage, which can make or break a good algorithm. Once again, if anything needs adjusting, I'm creating a copy. 

\- If an account actually survives all of that, and keep in mind this has been "testing" for around 2 months at this point, it gets moved to live trading on Alpaca or Robinhood, depending on leverage.

And yes, I use leverage. Which leads me a very important tip, if you use leverage in your algorithm, and it's just not working for some reason, look into the leverage and you'll probably realize why it's not working. It's a very simple observation, but it took me months to realize it and once I did, everything turned green.

It's real simple, exits are determined by leverage, adjust your exits accordingly.

All that being said, I'm looking for investors if you're interested.😊

comments.author: curioussharma-007
comments.body:
Tested it on [FakeTrades.in](http://FakeTrades.in)

\--------

I got curious about your accuracy numbers so I ran the actual base rates. Pulled 554,025 stock-days from FakeTrades database (296 stocks, 8 years) and asked one question: how often does a stock touch these levels above its open with *zero* prediction involved — just by existing?

Here's what any random stock does on any random day:

* Above open by a tick: 92% of all days
* \+0.25% above open: 84%
* \+0.5% above open: 74%
* \+1% above open: 54%

Now filter to only volatile names (your "cherry-picked universe of 300 tailored to how I trade" — same idea): +0.5% hits 78% and +1% hits 62%. No model. No signals. That's just what jumpy stocks do before lunch.

Notice something? Your v1 numbers (98% for a penny, 89% for 0.25%, 65% for 0.5%) sit right on top of these base rates. You actually caught this yourself with the penny thing — you just stopped one threshold too early. And Charles 2.0's 91.9%/84.6% is what these same base rates look like in a universe wilder than mine (US small caps run way hotter than my NSE names). The universe is doing the predicting. Charles is taking the credit.

But here's the part that matters more than any accuracy number: touching a level isn't money. A stock can tag +0.5% at 9:31 and close down 3%. If you buy the open with a +0.5% take-profit, your many small wins have to pay for the days the stock *never* goes above open — and those are exactly the crash days, where you're holding to the close. Small wins, fat losses, minus slippage. I noticed your whole post has percentages everywhere and not one dollar of P&L. That's usually not an accident, even when it's not intentional.

Genuine questions, not a gotcha: what's Charles 2.0's actual dollar P&L after costs, over how many trades? And what happens on the miss days — where do those exit? Those two numbers are the whole story. The accuracy stuff is weather forecasting: "it will rain this year in Seattle" is a 99%-accurate prediction and worth nothing.

(Your process section is honestly the best part of the post — copies instead of edits, weeks of paper trading for slippage, be your own worst critic. That discipline is worth more than the algo.)

exactly; looking at charts, it seems obvious that if something starts going up, it should continue. was amongst one of the first few strategies i tested. 

I've tested enough variations & combinations of

1. 30sec, 1m, 3m, 5m, 10m, 15m, ....

3. consecutive higher highs and/or with higher lows
4. take profit in .05% increments from 0.25% to 5% with & without trailing

6. RSI, ATR, ADX, Moving Averages
7. TQQQ, UPRO, CBOE, IWM, ...

the bad days always outweighed the small good ones.

replies.author: Weird_Cookie1700
replies.body:
Momentum plays a lot into Charles’s success for picking the stocks out of his universe that are actually going to go up. Momentum is huge, but it’s not everything.

I’ve also noticed with all the tests that I’ve done, and all of the live test that I’ve done more importantly, that exiting on a timer actually increases your profit because you usually miss your targeted exit point and when the algorithm refreshes per your timer, it’s past your exit point and you actually make more money. It’s weird, but it works.

If you don’t have a trail being activated, you’re missing out on tons of money, but a trail is also where you can lose a lot of money if you don’t set the rehearsal at the right place. So technically you really wanna set your activation point at a very high level that way when your trail activates you’re not losing as much. That was the only thing I could find they could negate it.

And having more money invested into an account helps yes. I would suggest starting with at least $3000 for any strategy that you’re trying to do on a live account because of slippage and because of the PDT rules. But you don’t have to have $10,000. You can do it with less it just takes longer and you need to be more disciplined.

replies.author: Weird_Cookie1700
replies.body:
This is pretty good. You’re *almost* right.

I agree with everything you’ve said. And honestly, if it really were as simple as you’re making it out to be, I’d have never written the post.

The fact of the matter is though, it’s not. Yeah, the specified universe helps tremendously but it’s not a standalone printing machine. Man, that would be awesome if it was though.

And my pictures actually have the dollar amounts on them. There was a space for total dollar amount but I guess with all the changes it’s been replaced or moved or something. Either way, just take the round trip average and multiple it by the number of wins. It’s $66.01 profit last week for the current Charles 2.0 that picture is from.

And because of slippage is why I test the way I do, each stage drops the actual ROI because each stage gets more and more “real”.

Charles 2.0 doesn’t have a stop loss, flattens at 355pm est, and if he loses money he loses money on a trade he makes up for it on the other 3 he bought that morning. He predicts up to 5 stocks going up, usually buys all of them, holds till they meet the exit point. If they don’t go at least 1% above open the trail doesn’t activate.

Last night I changed it to only buying the highest confidence stock and increased ROI by a lot just because of compounding into 1 name instead of 3-5/day.

comments.author: Ioqua
comments.body:
I took a look at this hoping to find the bit of Charles that actually worked as it's an area I've been working on for some time.

I dug through the old Android app, the live dashboard/API, historical picks, Council logic and paper-trading accounts.

There may be something interesting here, but it’s not what the headline numbers suggest.

The **91.9% / 84.6% “accuracy”** is basically measuring whether a volatile stock trades **0.5% / 1% above its open at some point during the day**.

On the exposed data:

**Recent Charles picks**

* 94.7% touched the predicted direction intraday
* 48.1% actually closed in that direction
* average open-to-close: **-0.11%**

**Charles 2.0 backtest**

* 97.8% touched the predicted direction
* 46.0% closed in that direction
* average open-to-close: basically **0%**

So Charles may be good at finding stocks likely to make a decent intraday move.

That is not the same as predicting a profitable trade.

The more worrying bit is the trading performance.

Of **92 paper accounts that traded:**

**23 are up.**  
**69 are down.**  
**Median return: -3.3%.**

And all **14 accounts set to automatically follow Charles lost money**.

One account had **28 winners and 77 losers**.

The backtests also use some very generous assumptions. One old strategy literally used:

**buy at the close, sell at the next day’s high**

and the Charles 2.0 **+1,621% backtest** gets most of its apparent edge from simulated ultra-tight trailing exits, while the stocks themselves average roughly flat from open to close.

I also looked at the **Council of Charles**. Publicly, I can see 9/10 and 10/10 agreement and templated reasoning, but not the analyst weights, individual scores or how the 16 signals are actually combined.

So my takeaway isn’t “Charles is rubbish”.

It’s that there may be a useful volatile-stock selection signal buried in there, but the headline accuracy and backtest returns don’t currently prove a tradable edge.

replies.author: Weird_Cookie1700
replies.body:
You’re mixing three different questions and then acting like you caught Charles in a lie.

1. “It only touched 0.5% / 1% above open.”  
 That’s the thing I already said in the post. Original Charles counted a penny over open as a hit. I called that unacceptable. That’s why 2.0 exists. Measuring “did it print 0.5% above open at some point” and calling it a gotcha is repeating my first paragraph.

2. “It didn’t close green / open-to-close is flat.”  
 That’s a hold-to-close test. Charles 2.0 is not a hold-to-close bot. It buys a specific way, trails a specific way, and is out the same day. If the edge is an intraday push and a trail, judging it by the 4:00 print is a different strategy. You can dislike that. You don’t get to relabel it as “no tradable edge” because close was flat.

3. “92 paper accounts, most red, all 14 auto-follow lost.”  
 That’s every test book you could see, including copies we already knew were dead, auto-follow from the old player product, and stuff that was never Charles 2.0. I said in the post we run a graveyard of algorithms on purpose and we don’t overwrite the ones that are live. Counting the graveyard as “Charles” is how you get 69 red books and a scary median. The 14 auto-follow books losing is not a secret either — that’s why that product isn’t the thing I’m talking about now.

4. “Backtest buys the close and sells the next day’s high” / “+1,621% is just a tight trail.”  
 One old test is not Charles 2.0. Tight trails on leveraged size are the point of the post you quoted: exits follow leverage. If you unwind that, of course the stocks look “about flat open to close.” That’s the same open-to-close trick again.

5. Council weights.  
 Yes, you can see 9/10 and 10/10 and you can’t see the weights. That’s the secret sauce line. Correct.

I’m not going to tell you Charles is magic or that every paper book prints. I’m telling you you graded a same-day trail system with close-to-close math, then averaged every failed experiment on the board and called it the product. That’s not due diligence. That’s a different bet.

If you want to argue the actual live 2.0 book — same-day, trail, flatten — argue that. Don’t flatten 90 test accounts and original Charles into one dunk.

replies.author: Ioqua
replies.body:
Dont take offence it's genuinely not meant, you are trying to find something very close to what I've been working at for months and fair point on the graveyard books and open-to-close. I’ll happily drop those as a direct measure of Charles 2.0.

But reading your own post again, I think the real issue is simpler.

As you said, Charles 2.0 is only a week old, made $66.01 last week, and you said you changed the strategy again last night to only take the highest-confidence pick because it backtested better.

So there isn’t really a frozen forward track record for the current 2.0 strategy yet, is there?

That’s all I’d want to see before taking the backtest seriously: freeze this version, leave the universe/entry/exit/leverage rules alone, and run it forward for a decent sample.

If it keeps producing after that, then fair play. That’s the interesting bit.

And again dont take it personally, I've pulled apart about 500+ hypotheses now looking for the magic one and this is just another I'm pulling apart.

replies.author: Weird_Cookie1700
replies.body:
No offense was taken, I just wanted to make sure the comparison is apples to apples.

Yes, Charles 2.0 is a week old and the variations of him (not pictured, the original Charles is what's pictured) are all on different strategies that are just offshoots of his main strategy.

I'm not sure how many live tests you've done but since I was able to package Charles into my mobile app, I was able to capture much more valuable information than any backtest can give anyone, because it was 6 months worth of live data. Using that data is how we made Charles 2.0, and he's already better than Charles, who was widely successful even without realizing it (man, I couldn't count the number of times I was like, well damn, I didn't know he did that) because he was using timers that missed marks but somehow luckily, when the timers fired they usually caught a better price.

So, to me, Charles 2.0 doesn't have to be thoroughly tested, because Charles already paved the way mostly, 2.0 is just trying to find the best way to drive on it.

I'd be interested to know what you've learned from the 500+ dissections because, and this is just from what you've written, the way you're dissecting them isn't entirely accurate which is going to skew your results in finding the magic one. Unless you know 100% about what the algo does, you can't really critique it the way you did with mine, because, like with mine, it won't work the right way.
